"So then the senior grabbed my bag," Kiran said, "and I just stared him down."
"Last week you said you pushed him," said Madhav.
"I did push him. A bit. After staring."
"And yesterday there were three seniors."
The others laughed. Kiran's face went hot. "There were three. Two were just watching."
On the way to the bus Madhav said quietly, "Kiran, I was there. He asked for his bag strap back, you gave it, and we walked off. That's it."
"Everyone was listening," Kiran said. "If I tell it like that, it's boring."
"But you have to remember which version you told to who. Doesn't that get tiring?"
Kiran didn't answer, just kicked a stone all the way to the bus stop.

qa.q: What did Madhav say really happened with the senior?
qa.a: Madhav said the senior asked for his bag strap back, Kiran gave it, and they walked off.

qa.q: How did Kiran feel when the others laughed, and why does the story keep growing?
qa.a: Kiran felt embarrassed, face going hot, and keeps making the story bigger out of worry that the plain version would seem boring to everyone listening.

qa.q: What could Kiran try the next time the group asks about the fight?
qa.a: Kiran could tell the plain version with a joke, trusting that people like Madhav value an honest story over a dramatic one.

qa.q: What is it like for Madhav to hear the story change each time?
qa.a: Madhav, who was there, finds it awkward and tiring, and cares enough to point out the cost privately rather than in front of everyone.

grounding: A teenager's story of a small clash with a senior grows each retelling to keep status, and a peer points out the strain of remembering every version.

I'm Rajni, and in Class 10 I became someone who couldn't just say a number. In the prelims I got 78 in maths. When Pooja's group asked, I said 88. By lunch it had become 90, "but the teacher cut marks unfairly". On the group call that night, it was 92.
The worst part wasn't the lie. It was the remembering. I had to keep track of which person had heard which version, and once I caught myself saying 88 to someone who had heard 92. My stomach dropped.
When the real mark sheets were put up, Pooja saw mine. She didn't say anything cruel. She just said, "You didn't need to." Looking back, the 78 would have been fine. It was the 92 I couldn't carry.

qa.q: What mark did Rajni actually get in maths in the prelims?
qa.a: Rajni got 78 in maths in the prelims.

qa.q: What does Rajni's stomach dropping suggest?
qa.a: It suggests fear of being caught, because keeping track of different versions for different people had become stressful.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could Rajni have done differently?
qa.a: Each retelling pushed the number higher until it couldn't be kept straight; saying 78 honestly at the start would have been far easier to carry.

qa.q: How might Pooja have felt when she saw the real mark sheet?
qa.a: Pooja seemed more sad than angry; her words "You didn't need to" suggest she would have accepted the real mark.

grounding: A teenager inflates a maths mark to impress peers, and the number grows with every retelling until remembering the versions becomes a burden.

Arnab, beta, you told your friends you beat the whole football team single-handed? Ha. Let your Rafiq Dada tell you about his own famous fight.
When I was fifteen, a senior pushed me in the school corridor. I pushed him back. That's all. Two pushes.
By evening, I'd told my friends I knocked him flat. The next day, I added that his two friends ran away. By the end of the week, there were three seniors, and I'd thrown one of them into the flowerbed. My friends looked at me like I was a hero.
Then, one afternoon, the senior himself walked up to our group and said, "Tell them what really happened." I couldn't even remember which version I'd told to whom. My mouth went dry. My friends slowly drifted away.
That flowerbed, beta, was the heaviest thing I ever carried.

qa.q: What did the senior do in the school corridor?
qa.a: The senior pushed him in the school corridor.

qa.q: How did young Rafiq feel when the senior asked him to tell what really happened?
qa.a: He felt panicked and ashamed, his mouth going dry, because he could not remember which stretched version he had told to whom.

qa.q: At which point in the story could Rafiq have stopped the story growing?
qa.a: On the first evening, when he told his friends, he could have simply said there were two pushes, before each retelling added more.

qa.q: How might Rafiq's friends have felt when the senior spoke up?
qa.a: They probably felt fooled and disappointed, which is why they slowly drifted away.

grounding: A grandfather recalls stretching a small fight into a heroic tale to impress his group, and how the story grew with each retelling until it collapsed.

The school bus back from the science exhibition was loud, hot, and stuck in traffic. Asif was squeezed next to Madhav in the back row with four other boys.
"So what did you get in the half-yearly?" one of them asked.
"Ninety-five in maths," Asif said. He had said ninety-two last week, to a different group. The real number was seventy-eight.
"Ninety-five? Show us," Madhav said, grinning. "Your mum sends the marks screenshot to everyone's parents anyway."
Asif's heart thumped. The class parents' group. He'd forgotten. By tonight, everyone would know.
He tried to remember what else he'd said. Had he told Madhav ninety-two, or eighty-nine? The bus lurched. The other boys were waiting.
Asif took a breath. "Actually, it's seventy-eight," he said, too loudly over the horns. "I kept adding numbers."
There was a pause. Then Madhav shrugged. "Seventy-eight's fine, man. I got sixty-one."

qa.q: What was Asif's real maths mark?
qa.a: The real number was seventy-eight.

qa.q: How was Asif feeling when Madhav mentioned the marks screenshot?
qa.a: Asif felt panicked, his heart thumping, because the stretched mark would soon be exposed and he could not keep track of his versions.

qa.q: What choice did Asif make, and why did it help?
qa.a: Asif told the real mark himself, which ended the need to remember different versions and turned out to cost little with his friends.

qa.q: How does Madhav react to the real mark?
qa.a: Madhav shrugs it off and shares his own lower mark, showing the group cared less about the number than Asif feared.

grounding: It shows a teenager inflating marks to keep status, the stretch growing each retelling until he must remember versions, and choosing the truth.

At the Saturday sleepover in Aparna's flat in Andheri, the girls lay in a row on the mattress, and Sonali told the story again.
Last week the version was simple: the college boy at the bus stop had smiled at her. On Tuesday, he had asked her name. Tonight, he had asked for her number, walked her home, and waited outside her building.
"Wait," Aparna said, propping herself up. "On Tuesday you said he just asked your name."
The room went quiet. Sonali's cheeks burned. "He… did both," she said. "I didn't tell you everything."
"Sonali, which is it?"
Sonali stared at the ceiling fan. She honestly couldn't remember anymore which details were real. The truth was a smile at a bus stop. That had felt like something once, before she made it bigger for them.
"He smiled," she said finally. "That's all. I just wanted it to be a better story."

qa.q: Where was the Saturday sleepover?
qa.a: At Aparna's flat in Andheri.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling when Aparna questioned the story?
qa.a: Sonali felt embarrassed and caught out, with burning cheeks, because she could not remember which details were real.

qa.q: What could Sonali try next time she wants to share something exciting?
qa.a: She could tell the small true version, like the smile, and trust that her friends care about her more than the size of the story.

qa.q: How does Aparna see Sonali's story changing?
qa.a: Aparna notices the details growing each week and feels confused, which makes her start to doubt what Sonali says.

grounding: It shows a teenager stretching a story about a crush to keep status with friends, the stretch growing until she cannot remember the real version.

"So wait," Harsha said. "Yesterday you said Aman asked for your number."
"He did. Well, he asked for the notes. And then he said 'thanks' in a really specific way."
"At lunch you told the girls he asked you to the fest."
Indu's ears went pink. "He said 'see you at the fest'. That's basically asking."
"And you told Mehr he wrote you a note."
"I didn't say note. I said message."
"You said note. With a heart."
Indu slumped against the locker. "Okay. It keeps getting bigger. Every time someone goes 'ooh', I add a bit. Now I can't remember which version I told who."
"Sounds exhausting."
"It is. And if Aman hears any of it, I'll die."
"So stop adding. Just say he's nice and you like him."
"That's so boring."
"It's also true," Harsha said.

qa.q: What did Aman actually ask Indu for?
qa.a: He asked for the notes.

qa.q: How does Indu feel about the growing story?
qa.a: Indu feels embarrassed and exhausted, unable to remember which version she told whom, and scared Aman will hear.

qa.q: What did Harsha suggest, and why might it help?
qa.a: Stop adding and just say Aman is nice and Indu likes him; one true version is easy to keep and won't embarrass her.

qa.q: How might Aman feel if he heard the stretched versions?
qa.a: Aman might feel awkward and misrepresented, hearing he'd asked Indu to the fest or sent a note with a heart when he hadn't.

grounding: Shows a teenager stretching a crush story to impress friends, the version growing with each retelling until it is hard to keep track.
